How much of the gain comes from the sources?
Stratified sampling, which uses only the sources' item difficulties, already gives $0.81$, $0.85$ and $0.83$ (interpolation, extrapolation, lineage), so it is the reference to beat.
Against it, the classes chosen without the outcomes (Table~\ref{tab:primary}, second block; Table~\ref{tab:lobo}) keep a gain of $0.80$--$0.88$ in interpolation and lineage, except anchors ($0.89$--$0.94$).
In extrapolation only the design-based class is clearly below stratified sampling ($0.91$ $[0.89,0.93]$, balanced $\times$ calibrated regression); the model-based ($1.00$ $[0.95,1.02]$) and difference-corrected classes ($1.03$ $[0.99,1.05]$) are not, and anchors and information selection are worse ($1.20$, $1.23$).
The gain needs the pairing of a source-informed design with a source-calibrated regression: the plain mean on the same balanced sample is $0.95$ $[0.93,0.97]$ of stratified sampling, and calibrated regression on a stratified or uniform sample is worse than their plain mean ($1.17$ and $1.23$).
The leave-one-benchmark-out step chooses the cell within a class, here balanced $\times$ calibrated regression on every held-out benchmark; naming this class as the one that beats stratified sampling is a second step among five classes on the same targets, so $0.91$ is the best of the five representatives, not a class the protocol selected.
The best cells, chosen after the outcomes, do slightly better (balanced $\times$ difference IRT $0.96$ $[0.93,0.99]$), and the classes chosen without them agree with those cells except for the difference-corrected class ($0.87$ against $0.82$ in extrapolation).
So the sources buy about a fifth of the error of a stratified sample when targets resemble them, and in extrapolation at most a tenth, which a balanced design with calibrated regression already delivers.
The gain comes mostly from the seven Open LLM Leaderboard benchmarks (balanced $\times$ difference IRT $0.71$ and $0.75$ of stratified sampling in interpolation and lineage); on the six HELM benchmarks, with about $80$ overlapping models each, it is $0.92$ and $1.00$ and the IRT model alone is no better than uniform ($0.95$ in interpolation; Table~\ref{tab:suite}).
With the top 10\% of models as targets the best difference cell reaches $0.70$ $[0.68,0.72]$ of uniform's error, with the top 50\% $0.96$ $[0.92,0.98]$, and uniform $\times$ difference IRT is barely below uniform ($0.97$ $[0.95,0.99]$).
At a budget of $2\%$ of each benchmark's items (between $9$ and $241$ items; Table~\ref{tab:twopct}) the pattern is the same and the sources buy more: the best difference cell is $0.69$ $[0.67,0.70]$ of stratified sampling in interpolation and $0.87$ $[0.85,0.89]$ in extrapolation, and the IRT model alone is $1.36$ times uniform in extrapolation. The classes chosen without the outcomes (leave-one-benchmark-out) are $0.63$--$0.73$ of stratified sampling in interpolation and, in extrapolation, $0.88$--$0.93$ for the info-top/CAT, design-based and difference-corrected classes, $0.96$ $[0.90,1.00]$ for anchors and $0.99$ $[0.94,1.01]$ for the model-based class.
With few source models the gain disappears (Figure~\ref{fig:msrc}): at $10$ sources balanced $\times$ difference IRT is $1.10$ and $1.04$ of uniform in interpolation and extrapolation, at $30$ it is $0.80$ and $0.86$, while stratified sampling, which needs the sources only to order items, hardly changes ($0.85$ to $0.81$ in interpolation).
